title: Partition, 1947
hookLine: Punjab is split; millions flee on both sides, many are killed, and Nankana Sahib is left in Pakistan

cards: Ask a Punjabi grandparent where the family comes from, and sometimes you get two answers: where we live now, and where we lived before.
Before might be a village near Lahore, or Rawalpindi, or Lyallpur, a place they never saw again. In August 1947, British rule in India ended, and the land was divided.

A new country, Pakistan, was made, and its border ran straight through the middle of Punjab. On one side, a family's fields, their well, their gurdwara. On the other, their new life, if they got there.

teach.h: A LINE DRAWN IN FIVE WEEKS.
teach.b: The line was drawn by a British lawyer, Cyril Radcliffe, who had never been to India, in about five weeks. It was published two days after independence, and millions of people woke up on the wrong side of it.
Muslims went west into Pakistan; Hindus and Sikhs went east into India. Across Punjab alone, something like ten million people crossed.
How many died, nobody knows exactly: estimates run from a few hundred thousand to perhaps two million. Trains arrived carrying the dead. Women were taken from their families.
And this lesson holds on to one thing: the violence came from every side.

teach.h: NO PEOPLE AS A WHOLE TO BLAME.
teach.b: Muslims, Hindus and Sikhs all suffered, and people from every community did terrible things, so no people as a whole is to blame.

There are also stories, on both sides of the line, of neighbors who hid neighbors and walked them to safety. For Sikhs there was a particular loss. Punjab was the land of the Gurus, and the line cut it in half.
Nankana Sahib, where Guru Nanak was born, was now in Pakistan. So was Kartarpur, where he farmed and died, and Panja Sahib, and the place in Lahore where Guru Arjan was martyred.
In Punjabi, Partition is often called simply the vand, the division. For many families it isn't history at all. It's a grandmother's silence in August, a village name said softly at a kitchen table.

how: Sikh families remember Partition in stories passed down at home, and the daily Ardas asks for open access to the gurdwaras left in Pakistan; groups of Sikh pilgrims travel there for gurpurabs.

games.q: it's august 1947. you're a Sikh farmer, and the new line puts your village in Pakistan. what do most families like yours do?
o: stay and wait for things to calm down.
leave nearly everything and head east to India.
move to a big city inside Pakistan.
games.why: most Sikh and Hindu families in west Punjab left, often with only what they could carry. neighbors on both sides sometimes helped them get out.

practice: Think of a family split by a border, a war, a move or a quarrel, from 1947 or your own, and picture a table with one empty chair kept for someone on the other side.
If you pray, hold them in your prayer, in whatever words are already yours; if you don't, keep them in mind and wish them safe. When your thoughts drift, come back to the chair.

wordCard.voice: Partition. The division of 1947, when a line split Punjab between India and Pakistan, and millions crossed it. In Punjabi, often just the vand.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: vand, division; the same word as in vand chhakna, sharing what you have.
